source.title: Understanding double descent through the lens of principal component regression

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes double descent in linear regression and reports synthetic test-error sweeps, using PCR theory rather than testing the original deep-network method.
record.gate_note: The study tests model-capacity risk behavior in synthetic linear regression. It does not test epoch-wise descent or increasing the regression training-set size near interpolation. Its face experiments report representation-dependent regression performance, not a separate explicit test of the double-descent curve. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Theoretical PCR analysis of minimum-norm overparameterized linear regression, with synthetic sweeps of test RMSE against feature count (Fig. 4b). These bear on V4: risk improving past interpolation in a non-deep model class. No deep networks, epoch sweeps or sample-size sweeps are run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that final second-descent linear regression equals PCR with all PCs, and that PCR lower-bounds the whole double-descent risk curve. If the smallest singular value exceeds an SNR threshold, final second descent beats any linearly transformed first- or second-descent model. Second-descent models are equivalent to first-descent models that approach PCR. They apply this to explain the other-race effect, with face-feature experiments they say bear out the hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical PCR analysis and synthetic linear-regression simulations, rather than the original deep-network model-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The smallest singular value, and thus the study's SNR condition, changes whether the PCR lower bound is tight and how the risk curve behaves.

fits_no_version.finding: Rotating the feature representation away from PCs (noise added to V, or PCA on an extended data set) raises RMSE in both descents. The final second-descent solution is invariant to these manipulations (Fig. 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Peak height and second-descent quality in linear regression depend on how well the features align with the training PCs; the final interpolating solution is invariant to such rotations.

fits_no_version.finding: Lemma 2 and the Discussion argue every second-descent regression equals some first-descent regression on at most m transformed features. Improvement in the second descent reflects these models approaching exact PCR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Second-descent solutions in linear regression are reparameterized first-descent models whose risk is lower-bounded by PCR. This is a theoretical analogue of V7 with no effective-parameter replot.

record.problems: Evidence for the claim is limited to linear regression. The plotted RMSE values are not tabulated, and the synthetic curves average over 25 design matrices. The study does not test epochs or regression training-sample-size sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows retained. Figures 1 and 3 and Appendix Figures 6–7 report modified-representation or race-dependent regression results, but the text emphasizes representation degradation or same-race advantages rather than explicitly testing the general double-descent shape.

untested.parts: Deep-network model-wise double descent; only linear regression is simulated.
Model classes other than linear/PCR regression.
A single effective-complexity predictor of peak location across axes.
Label-noise variation, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned regularization. SNR is varied only through σm with σy fixed, and only in PCR (Fig. 4a), which no row records.
No empirical replot against an effective parameter count. Lemma 2 argues every second-descent solution equals a first-descent (rank ≤ m) solution, but this is theory only.

missing.what: PCR risk curves for σm ∈ {0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75}. Lower SNRm gives a more U-shaped curve as the smallest PCs degrade performance. This bears on the U-shape vs second-descent part of V4 and on the SNR dependence of V6.
RMSE vs number of parameters under rotated or extended PC representations. Shows degraded first and second descent, with the final second-descent solution invariant.
Real-data RMSE vs number of parameters across first and second descent for VGG16 and AAM face features. The curve shape is not described beyond same-race being better throughout.

record.verdict_notes: SNRm = σm²·(||β||²/m)/σy², with ||β||²/m = 1 and σy = 0.5. This gives SNRm ≈ 0.04, 0.25, 1 and 2.25 for R1–R4. Only R3 and R4 meet the stated tightness condition, which motivates splitting the labels. All row values are figure-only, and the interpolation peak is not quantified. The Fig. 1 caption ('SNRm = 0.5') appears inconsistent with the Fig. 4 σm values. The study is a bioRxiv preprint, not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Increasing the number of regression training samples near interpolation.
Only synthetic linear regression is tested; the study does not test other model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The study varies the smallest singular value with label-noise level held fixed; it does not test label-noise variation, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not measure risk against an effective parameter count to determine whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Synthetic min-norm linear regression with SNRm ≥ 1 (σm = 0.5, 0.75)
relationships.reason: The text says final second descent is optimal and attains the PCR lower bound in these settings, so risk improves again past interpolation (R3, R4; values figure-only).
relationships.display_finding: The final second descent achieved optimal risk and attained the PCR lower bound in the specified signal-to-noise settings.

relationships.reason: Below the SNR threshold the final second descent is not guaranteed best and the lower bound is not tight, so the second-descent benefit depends on the smallest singular value (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: The final second descent was not guaranteed to be best, and the lower bound was not tight, making its benefit sensitive to the smallest singular value.
